article_title: ICT-support for grounding in the classroom
citation: Pieter J. Beers, Paul A. Kirschner, Henny P. A. Boshuizen, Wim H. Gijselaers. (2007). ICT-support for grounding in the classroom. Instructional Science 35, 535–556. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9018-5
title: NTool: an ICT communication tool with an embedded negotiation formalism and two coercion levels
description: NTool is an online, newsgroup-reader-based communication tool for asynchronous, text-based discussion that directly supports grounding by making users externalise their private understanding of others' contributions. "The formalism consists of negotiation primitives, basic building blocks that constitute a speciﬁc dialogue model" — contribution, verification, clarification, acceptance/rejection, and position — with five rules (Table 1) prescribing their use. Two script implementations were used: the Idiosyncratic version offered primitives without coercive rules, while the Stringent version, "applied strict rules for the situations in which each message type could and could not be used," greying out unavailable options.
requirements: Participants receive a tutorial and practice case on the formalism before use (75 min practice phase)
constraints: Coercion in both implementations was aimed at the verification and clarification primitives only; no measures of actual individual learning or task performance were taken in the study
target_learners: secondary vocational education students in multidisciplinary three-person teams
target_learning_goals: negotiation of common ground during collaborative complex problem-solving
examples: 22 teams used NTool to make a functional design of floating housing as a solution for sea-level rise, in two sessions with individual pre-tests and post-tests
key_sources: Pieter J. Beers, Paul A. Kirschner, Henny P. A. Boshuizen, Wim H. Gijselaers. (2007). ICT-support for grounding in the classroom. Instructional Science 35, 535–556. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9018-5

article_title: Conventional twin studies overestimate the environmental differences between families relevant to educational attainment
citation: Wolfram, T. & Morris, D. (2023). Conventional twin studies overestimate the environmental differences between families relevant to educational attainment. npj Science of Learning 8, 24. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00173-y
title: Nuclear Twin and Family Design (NTFD) as a framework for relaxing Classical Twin Design assumptions
description: The NTFD extends the CTD by adding parents and non-twin siblings, allowing assortative mating to be modelled directly (via phenotypic assortment or social homogamy), non-additive genetic influences and shared environment to be estimated simultaneously, and the shared environment to be decomposed into sibling-shared (S), parental transmission (P), and twin-specific (T) components. The article states that "Including additional relative classes in the NTFD enables several of the assumptions in the CTD to be relaxed and more parameters to be estimated." It is used to quantify bias in CTD ACE estimates of educational attainment.
requirements: Data on twins, their parents, and non-twin siblings from the same families
Assumptions about the source of spousal resemblance (phenotypic assortment vs social homogamy) that cannot all be estimated simultaneously
constraints: Only two of phenotypic transmission, non-additive genetic effects, and sibling-shared environments can be estimated at once, so baseline models fix one to zero
The biases reported for educational attainment will not necessarily generalise to other traits
target_learners: adult twins and their siblings and parents in longitudinal family studies
target_learning_goals: decomposing genetic and environmental sources of variance in educational attainment
examples: Applied to 982 German TwinLife families, contrasting PA ASTE (A = 51%) with the CTD (A = 34%) on the same data
key_sources: Wolfram, T. & Morris, D. (2023). Conventional twin studies overestimate the environmental differences between families relevant to educational attainment. npj Science of Learning 8, 24. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00173-y

article_title: The relationship of school performance with self-control and grit is strongly genetic and weakly causal
citation: Kevenaar, S. T., van Bergen, E., Oldehinkel, A. J., Boomsma, D. I. & Dolan, C. V. (2023). The relationship of school performance with self-control and grit is strongly genetic and weakly causal. npj Science of Learning, 8:53. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00198-3
title: Netherlands Twin Register teacher-rating dataset on self-control, grit, and school performance in 12-year-old twins
description: A dataset from the Netherlands Twin Register comprising teacher ratings of grit, self-control, and school performance for 11.5–12.5-year-old twins, including 3837 complete pairs and 1054 incomplete pairs, with data on 8728 individuals (1957 MZ and 2934 DZ pairs). Self-control was measured with the 8-item Achenbach Self-Control Scale (Cronbach's alpha 0.87), grit with three teacher-rated perseverance items (alpha 0.90), and school performance as the sum of teacher ratings of math, reading, and literacy (alpha 0.84), which correlated 0.70 with the CITO standardized test.
requirements: Parental permission to contact teachers; zygosity established by DNA or blood test for 32.2% of same-sex pairs and by parental questionnaire (over 96% accuracy) otherwise
constraints: All measures are teacher ratings, which the article acknowledges may be biased by teachers' awareness of students' school performance; ceiling effects required right-censored maximum likelihood modelling
target_learning_goals: Measuring non-cognitive skills (self-control, perseverance) and academic school performance
examples: Data collection was approved by the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam ethics committee (VCWE-2021-111) with parental written informed consent
key_sources: Kevenaar, S. T., van Bergen, E., Oldehinkel, A. J., Boomsma, D. I. & Dolan, C. V. (2023). The relationship of school performance with self-control and grit is strongly genetic and weakly causal. npj Science of Learning, 8:53. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00198-3

article_title: The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations
citation: Michael J. Baker. (2015). The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0050-3
title: NTD model of negotiation in teaching-learning dialogues
description: The NTD model represents negotiation between tutor and learner as movement from initial to final states in which agents share the goal of reaching agreement on 'negotia', the objects of negotiation. Parties make offers that are successively refined, and the refine strategy was defined in terms of two main elements: "communicative acts of negotiation, and transformation functions". Crucially, communicative acts are proposals with acceptances or rejections, not assertions, so participants express what they are willing to accept rather than their beliefs. The article presents this as the retained core of a research programme later extended to argumentation, affect and CSCL.
requirements: Dialogue participants who make proposals that can be accepted, rejected or refined rather than asserted as beliefs
constraints: The published model detailed only the refine strategy; the argue strategy was deferred to later work, so it addressed knowledge refinement processes in negotiation rather than full negotiation
target_learners: students in tutorial dialogue with a computer tutor
target_learning_goals: reaching shared agreement on task-level knowledge such as problem solutions and their justifications
examples: The KANT prototype engaged students in negotiative dialogue about musical structure analysis and justifications
key_sources: Michael J. Baker. (2015). The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0050-3

article_title: Training technical or non-technical skills: an arbitrary distinction? A scoping review.
citation: Gamborg ML, Salling LB, Rölfing JD, Jensen RD. (2024). Training technical or non-technical skills: an arbitrary distinction? A scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06419-6
title: Non-technical skills as a poorly defined construct in need of reconceptualization, with knowledge not qualifying as a skill
description: The review argues that NTS is poorly defined and therefore harder than TS to assess, noting that despite work on behavioural markers, consensus definitions and taxonomies, "there is still little consensus on how to assess NTS". During analysis the authors found several publications defining knowledge as an NTS; they argue knowledge "refers to the process of expanding a frame of mind, rather than an applicable skill" and is the foundation actions are based on rather than a skill itself, and they excluded studies defining knowledge as NTS without assessing other NTS aspects.
requirements: Research should validate the tools they use to assess NTS, using well established frameworks such as Kane's validity framework
constraints: Unclear definitions of NTS in the literature were an obstacle; the review applied a broad definition of NTS as all skills that are not body-kinetic skills, excluding knowledge-only studies
target_learners: healthcare professionals and physicians in medical education
target_learning_goals: accurate conceptualization and valid assessment of non-technical skills
examples: The review's broad working definition incorporated personal resources skills and cognitive skills in addition to traditionally defined NTS such as teamwork and communication.
key_sources: Gamborg ML, Salling LB, Rölfing JD, Jensen RD. (2024). Training technical or non-technical skills: an arbitrary distinction? A scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06419-6

article_title: The impact of intraoperative non-technical skills training on scrub practitioners' self-efficacy: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Mohammadi Masoumeh, Omid Athar, Tarrahi Mohammad Javad, Ghadami Ahmad. (2025). The impact of intraoperative non-technical skills training on scrub practitioners' self-efficacy: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07042-9
title: Incorporate non-technical skills training into scrub practitioner curricula and continuing education
description: Based on the trial's finding that training enhanced self-efficacy, the authors conclude "it is necessary to incorporate non-technical skills training into the educational curriculum and continuing education programs for scrub practitioners". They argue non-technical skills are crucial for safe, efficient task performance and that such programs could improve patient safety and reduce surgical errors, particularly given that NTS have been overlooked in nursing education and that the Middle East and North Africa region shows increasing need for this training.
requirements: Curriculum space and continuing-education structures for scrub practitioners; SPLINTS-based content with validated translation
constraints: Evidence covers short-term self-efficacy only; long-term sustainability not yet assessed, and task-management self-efficacy did not improve significantly
target_learners: Scrub practitioners and operating room nurses
target_learning_goals: Intraoperative non-technical skills and related self-efficacy
examples: The RCT trained intervention-group practitioners in two two-hour sessions during regular working hours at two Iranian public hospitals
key_sources: Mohammadi Masoumeh, Omid Athar, Tarrahi Mohammad Javad, Ghadami Ahmad. (2025). The impact of intraoperative non-technical skills training on scrub practitioners' self-efficacy: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07042-9

article_title: Non-technical skills simulation-based training model for managing intraoperative posterior capsule rupture during cataract surgery.
citation: Wood Thomas Charles, Maqsood Sundas, Saunders Alex, Sancha William, Nanavaty Mayank A., Wearne Michael, Rajak Saul. (2022). Non-technical skills simulation-based training model for managing intraoperative posterior capsule rupture during cataract surgery. Eye. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41433-022-01962-2
title: Fully immersive NTS-focused PCR simulation-based training model (two identical simulations separated by an interactive training intervention)
description: A high-fidelity simulation model in which surgeons manage an intraoperative posterior capsule rupture in a fully equipped operating theatre, with "extensive NTS stressors designed to challenge the surgeon’s handling of the case". The model "consisted of two identical PCR simulations with NTS stressors applied, separated by a predominantly NTS focussed training intervention" delivered as three remote presentations co-developed with a commercial aviation pilot. Performance was assessed with HUFOES and OSATS by blinded assessors.
requirements: Minimum faculty of one scrub nurse, one wandering nurse and one simulation coordinator, with faculty knowing the intended complication events, NTS stressors and responses to potential outcomes
A recorded pilot of the scenario and iterative focus-group revisions to establish realism, feasibility, deliverability and content validity
constraints: The primary limitation is the financial and time expense of using operating theatres, staff, equipment and set-up
Handmade simulation eyes occasionally needed replacing mid-scenario due to severe posterior chamber positive pressure
The model was not considered to prepare trainees for independent PCR management if imminently encountered in reality
target_learners: Ophthalmic surgeons of all training grades
target_learning_goals: Non-technical skills for managing intraoperative posterior capsule rupture, including leadership, communication, situational awareness and stress management
examples: Seventeen cataract surgeons from four hospitals in the Kent, Surrey and Sussex region completed the scenario, with videos recorded on ZEISS Callisto and smots camera systems and emailed to participants for personal reflection
key_sources: Wood Thomas Charles, Maqsood Sundas, Saunders Alex, Sancha William, Nanavaty Mayank A., Wearne Michael, Rajak Saul. (2022). Non-technical skills simulation-based training model for managing intraoperative posterior capsule rupture during cataract surgery. Eye. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41433-022-01962-2
